_comment: GENERATED consolidation of six small canonical reference files (source metadata preserved verbatim under each key). Built by tools/export_reference_pack.py — never edit by hand.

blooms_taxonomy._comment: Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). Six cognitive process dimensions with action verbs. Used by cognitive-rigor atom to classify objectives and assessment items. Source: public-domain summary of the published taxonomy.
blooms_taxonomy.source: Anderson, L.W. & Krathwohl, D.R. (2001). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing.

levels.name: Remember
levels.definition: Retrieve relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

levels.name: Understand
levels.definition: Construct meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

levels.name: Apply
levels.definition: Carry out or use a procedure in a given situation.

levels.name: Analyze
levels.definition: Break material into constituent parts and determine how parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

levels.name: Evaluate
levels.definition: Make judgments based on criteria and standards.

levels.name: Create
levels.definition: Put elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganize elements into a new pattern or structure.

knowledge_dimensions.description: Basic elements students must know — terminology, specific details.
Interrelationships among basic elements — categories, principles, theories.
How to do something — methods, techniques, algorithms, criteria for use.
Knowledge of cognition and awareness of one's own cognition.

webbs_dok._comment: Webb's Depth of Knowledge (DOK) framework. Four complexity levels for aligning standards, instruction, and assessment. Used by cognitive-rigor atom alongside Bloom's. Source: Norman Webb (1997, 2002), WCEPS. Public framework.
webbs_dok.source: Webb, N.L. (1997). Criteria for Alignment of Expectations and Assessments. CCSSO/WCEPS.

levels.name: Recall & Reproduction
levels.description: Recall a fact, definition, term, or perform a simple procedure. Requires rote responses, use of formulas, or one-step processes.
levels.student_role: The student recalls, observes, or completes a routine task.

examples.ELA: Identify the setting of a story.
examples.Math: Recall the formula for area of a rectangle.
examples.Science: Label the parts of a cell.

levels.assessment_ceiling: Selected-response items testing isolated facts or simple procedures.

levels.name: Skill / Concept
levels.description: Requires mental processing beyond recall — decisions about how to approach a problem, requires two or more steps.
levels.student_role: The student makes decisions about approach, classifies, organizes, compares, or interprets information.

examples.ELA: Compare two characters' motivations using text evidence.
examples.Math: Solve a two-step word problem choosing the correct operations.
examples.Science: Classify organisms based on observable characteristics.

levels.assessment_ceiling: Short constructed-response items, items requiring application of a concept.

levels.name: Strategic Thinking
levels.description: Requires reasoning, planning, developing a plan or sequence of steps. Requires justification, complex and abstract thinking.
levels.student_role: The student reasons, plans, uses evidence, thinks abstractly. More than one possible answer.

examples.ELA: Write an argument using multiple sources and address a counterclaim.
examples.Math: Solve a non-routine problem requiring multiple approaches.
examples.Science: Design an experiment to test a hypothesis.

levels.assessment_ceiling: Extended constructed-response, multi-step problems with justification.

levels.name: Extended Thinking
levels.description: Requires investigation, complex reasoning over time, and connecting and applying multiple concepts. Typically takes days or weeks.
levels.student_role: The student connects and synthesizes ideas across content areas, applies knowledge to real-world problems.

examples.ELA: Write a research paper synthesizing multiple perspectives on a social issue.
examples.Math: Design and conduct a statistical study to answer a real-world question.
examples.Science: Conduct a multi-week investigation, analyze data, and present findings.

levels.assessment_ceiling: Performance tasks, research projects, portfolios — rarely used in on-demand testing.

webbs_dok.alignment_note: A standard's DOK is the CEILING — the most complex thinking the standard demands. Assessment items should match the standard's DOK, not default to DOK 1. Use alongside Bloom's: Bloom's identifies the cognitive PROCESS; DOK identifies the COMPLEXITY of that process.

cast_udl_3_0._comment: CAST Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Guidelines 3.0 (July 2024). 3 principles, 9 guidelines, 31 checkpoints. Used by udl-options and accommodation-match atoms. Source: udlguidelines.cast.org. Licensed under Creative Commons BY-SA 4.0.
cast_udl_3_0.source: CAST (2024). Universal Design for Learning Guidelines version 3.0. https://udlguidelines.cast.org
cast_udl_3_0.goal: Develop expert learners who are purposeful and motivated, resourceful and knowledgeable, and strategic and goal-directed.

principles.description: The WHY of learning. Provide multiple means of engagement to tap into learners' interests, challenge them appropriately, and motivate them.

checkpoints.text: Heighten salience of goals and objectives
Vary demands and resources to optimize challenge
Promote expectations and beliefs that optimize motivation
Facilitate personal coping skills and strategies

principles.description: The WHAT of learning. Provide multiple means of representation to give learners various ways of acquiring information and knowledge.

checkpoints.text: Offer ways of customizing the display of information
Support decoding of text, mathematical notation, and symbols
Highlight patterns, critical features, big ideas, and relationships

principles.description: The HOW of learning. Provide multiple means of action and expression to allow learners alternatives for demonstrating what they know.

checkpoints.text: Vary the methods for response and navigation
Optimize access to tools and assistive technologies
Use multiple tools for construction and composition
Build fluencies with graduated levels of support for practice and performance

fl_feaps._comment: Florida Educator Accomplished Practices (FEAPs). 6 practices with indicators per Rule 6A-5.065, F.A.C. Used by professional-learning and school-administration atoms for observation alignment. Source: FLDOE (revised June 2025). Public data.
fl_feaps.source: Florida Department of Education. Rule 6A-5.065, F.A.C. https://www.fldoe.org/teaching/professional-dev/the-fl-educator-accomplished-practices.stml

practices.name: Instructional Design and Lesson Planning
practices.description: Applying concepts from human development and learning theories, the effective educator consistently designs standards-based lessons, plans instruction, and selects strategies to engage and meet the needs of learners.
indicators: Aligns instruction with state-adopted standards at the appropriate level of rigor
Sequences lessons and concepts to ensure coherence and required prior knowledge
Designs instruction for students to achieve mastery
Selects appropriate formative assessments to monitor learning
Uses diagnostic student data to plan lessons
Develops learning experiences that require students to demonstrate a variety of applicable skills and competencies

practices.name: The Learning Environment
practices.description: To maintain a student-centered learning environment that is safe, organized, equitable, flexible, inclusive, and collaborative, the effective educator consistently arranges and manages the physical and social conditions of the learning environment.
indicators: Organizes, allocates, and manages the resources of time, space, and attention
Manages individual and class behaviors through a well-planned management system
Conveys high expectations to all students
Respects students' cultural, linguistic, and family background
Models clear, acceptable oral and written communication skills
Maintains a climate of openness, inquiry, fairness, and support
Integrates current information and communication technologies
Adapts the learning environment to accommodate the differing needs and diversity of students
Utilizes current and emerging assistive technologies that enable students to participate in high-quality communication and interaction

practices.name: Instructional Delivery and Facilitation
practices.description: The effective educator consistently utilizes a deep and comprehensive knowledge of the subject taught to deliver engaging and relevant lessons and facilitate student achievement.
indicators: Delivers engaging and challenging lessons
Deepens and enriches students' understanding through content area literacy strategies, verbalization of thought, and application of the subject matter
Identifies gaps in students' subject matter knowledge
Modifies instruction to respond to preconceptions or misconceptions
Relates and integrates the subject matter with other disciplines and life experiences
Employs higher-order questioning techniques
Applies varied instructional strategies and resources, including appropriate technology
Differentiates instruction based on an assessment of student learning needs and recognition of individual differences
Supports, encourages, and provides immediate and specific feedback to students to promote student achievement
Utilizes student feedback to monitor instructional needs and to adjust instruction

practices.name: Assessment
practices.description: The effective educator consistently gathers, analyzes, and uses data and evidence to inform decisions about teaching and learning.
indicators: Analyzes and applies data from multiple assessments and measures
Designs and aligns formative and summative assessments that match learning objectives and lead to mastery
Uses a variety of assessment tools to monitor student progress, achievement, and learning gains
Modifies assessments and testing conditions to accommodate learning styles and varying levels of knowledge
Shares the importance and outcomes of student assessment data with the student and the student's parent/caregiver(s)
Applies technology to organize and integrate assessment information

practices.name: Continuous Professional Improvement
practices.description: The effective educator consistently designs purposeful professional goals to strengthen the effectiveness of instruction based on students' needs.
indicators: Designs purposeful professional goals to strengthen the effectiveness of instruction based on students' needs
Examines and uses data-informed research to improve instruction and student achievement
Uses a variety of data, independently and in collaboration with colleagues, to evaluate learning outcomes, adjust planning, and continuously improve the effectiveness of lessons
Collaborates with the home, school, and larger communities to foster communication and to support student learning and continuous improvement
Applies knowledge of emerging trends in education to enhance professional practice

practices.name: Professional Responsibility and Ethical Conduct
practices.description: Understanding that educators are held to a high moral standard in a community, the effective educator adheres to the Code of Ethics and the Principles of Professional Conduct of the Education Profession of Florida.
indicators: Understands and adheres to the Code of Ethics and Principles of Professional Conduct
Fulfills the expected obligations to students, the public, and the education profession

coxhead_awl._comment: Coxhead Academic Word List (AWL). 570 word families in 10 sublists ordered by frequency in academic texts. Used by vocabulary-select atom for identifying academic vocabulary. Source: Coxhead, A. (2000). Victoria University of Wellington. Public data.
coxhead_awl.source: Coxhead, A. (2000). A New Academic Word List. TESOL Quarterly 34(2), pp.213-238.
